claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 forms a homogeneous high-temperature BCC state after solution treatment at approximately 1300°C.
Slow cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for chemical ordering.
Slow cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for Al partitioning.
Chemical ordering and Al partitioning lower the local Gibbs free energy.
The reduction in local Gibbs free energy triggers transformation to a more thermodynamically stable phase.
Rapid quenching kinetically freezes the high-temperature BCC state despite an underlying thermodynamic driving force for transformation.
Al partitioning and chemical ordering occur at incipient secondary-phase interfaces during slow cooling.
Enhanced atomic diffusion during slow cooling causes Al, and potentially other elements, to segregate.
Elemental segregation promotes local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering lowers the nucleation barrier for formation of an FCC or intermetallic secondary phase.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and kinetically traps the BCC state.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit more secondary-phase nucleation than rapidly quenched samples.
Secondary-phase regions in slow-cooled samples will show enhanced chemical order and Al enrichment.
Rapidly quenched samples will remain largely in the metastable high-temperature BCC state.
The proposed controlled comparison is rapid quenching in less than 1 second versus cooling at 1°C/min to approximately 600°C after identical homogenization at 1300°C.
The cooling-rate mechanism is expected to apply when grain size, residual stress, recrystallization, and grain growth are controlled sufficiently to isolate thermal-history effects.
A lack of any significant increase in ordering, Al segregation, or secondary-phase formation in slow-cooled samples relative to quenched controls would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis distinguishes a pre-existing thermodynamic driving force from cooling-rate-controlled kinetics, whereas the falsification rule describes slow cooling as enhancing the thermodynamic driving force. Slow cooling is otherwise said to increase diffusion, ordering, and nucleation rather than to create the underlying thermodynamic force.
